criteria.quote: Goldeen looks elegant, but competes for the sharpest horn.
criteria.revision: Change the opening to: "Goldeen is called the Water Queen for its fins—but Goldeen apparently compete over whose horn is thickest and sharpest." This creates a sharper contrast while avoiding the unsupported idea that they are actively growing their horns.

criteria.quote: Its dress-like fins earned it the name Water Queen.
criteria.revision: Make the specificity denser by pairing the nickname with the exact horn detail: "Its dress-like tail fin earned it the name Water Queen—but apparently, Goldeen compete to see whose horn is thickest and sharpest."

criteria.quote: Why does Goldeen's elegant look come with a horn contest?
criteria.revision: Replace the causal "Why" with an evidence-grounded contrast the story can answer: "If Goldeen's fins make it the Water Queen, why are its horns the feature it apparently compares?"

criteria.quote: That pretty swimmer can ram powerfully with its horn.
criteria.revision: Replace this scene with a new escalation: "The water dancer is also a strong swimmer, capable of moving nonstop up fast streams at five knots." Then follow with the researched glass-shattering ram, before revealing the horn competition.

criteria.quote: It can even shatter the thickest glass with one horn ram.
criteria.revision: Delay the explicit competition reveal until the final third, and change the title to "Goldeen's Fins Aren't the Whole Story." This preserves the glass surprise and makes the later thickest-and-sharpest horn detail a stronger change in perspective.

criteria.quote: Goldeen looks elegant, but competes for the sharpest horn.; That pretty swimmer can ram powerfully with its horn.; Goldeen compete to see whose horn is thickest and sharpest.
criteria.revision: Give the middle scenes distinct functions: use the Water Queen nickname for appearance, five knots for athletic ability, the glass ram for force, and only then the thickest-and-sharpest competition as the social standard.

criteria.quote: Its fins make it a water princess, while its horn makes elegance feel dangerous.
criteria.revision: End with the researched contrast rather than a general danger statement: "Its fins earn it the name Water Queen, but the feature Goldeen apparently compete over is the horn: whose is thickest and sharpest?"

criteria.quote: Which wins your attention: Goldeen's fins or its horn?
criteria.revision: Make the closing question a genuine evidence-based split: "Is Goldeen defined more by the fins that earn it the name Water Queen—or by the horn it apparently competes to make thickest and sharpest?"
